## Part 1: Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1: Load the Data and Make a Point Pattern

::: {.why}
We'll use fire station locations in Forsyth, Guilford and Alamance counties (Winston-Salem, Greensboro and Burlington). `spatstat` needs a point pattern (`ppp`): the points plus a window, which is the area where points could have been. Here the window is the three counties. The data are in NC State Plane (feet), so `rescale.ppp()` turns the units into miles.
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(spatstat)

#NC counties, projected to NC State Plane (feet)
nc_counties <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1hXVtKL_33c4QRw6_Z9LlYqjgisdYCRqX") |>
  st_transform(2264)

#fire stations (already in NC State Plane)
stations <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1bjAeEaoVZUjf9VLJTKl_anABwznioAoa")
```

```{r}
#the three counties are the window
triad <- nc_counties |>
  filter(county_name %in% c("Forsyth County, North Carolina",
                            "Guilford County, North Carolina",
                            "Alamance County, North Carolina"))

#keep the stations inside the window
stations <- st_filter(stations, triad)

#make the point pattern, convert feet to miles, and drop exact duplicates
station_pp <- as.ppp(st_geometry(stations), W = as.owin(st_union(triad)))
station_pp <- rescale.ppp(station_pp, 5280, "mile")
station_pp <- unique(station_pp)
station_pp
```

### Step 2: Look at Intensity (First Order)

::: {.why}
First-order structure is about how the intensity, the number of points per square mile, changes across the window. A kernel density map shows it.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "Kernel density map of fire stations in Forsyth, Guilford and Alamance counties, with the stations drawn as points. Density is highest in central Greensboro and central Winston-Salem and lowest in the rural edges of the counties."}
plot(density(station_pp), main = "Fire stations per square mile")
plot(station_pp, add = TRUE, pch = 16, cex = 0.5)
```

### Step 3: Quadrat Test

::: {.why}
Split the window into quadrats and count the points in each. Under complete spatial randomness (CSR), each quadrat expects a count in proportion to its area, and for equal-sized quadrats the variance-to-mean ratio (VMR) is about 1. A VMR well above 1 means uneven intensity. The Monte Carlo test compares the counts with 999 random patterns.
:::

```{r, fig.alt = "The three-county window split into six quadrats, with the number of fire stations printed in each. The counts range widely, with the most stations in the quadrats that hold Greensboro and Winston-Salem."}
set.seed(391)

station_q <- quadratcount(station_pp, nx = 3, ny = 2)
plot(station_pp, pch = 16, cex = 0.5, main = "Fire stations per quadrat")
plot(station_q, add = TRUE, col = "black", cex = 1.4)

#variance-to-mean ratio
var(as.vector(station_q)) / mean(as.vector(station_q))

quadrat.test(station_pp, nx = 3, ny = 2, method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
```

### Step 4: Average Nearest Neighbor (Second Order)

::: {.why}
Second-order structure is about how points relate to each other. The average nearest neighbor (ANN) ratio divides the observed mean distance to the nearest point by the distance expected under CSR. A ratio below 1 means clustered, about 1 means random and above 1 means dispersed. `clarkevans.test()` gives the same ratio (R) and a p-value from 999 random patterns in the same window.
:::

```{r}
set.seed(391)

#observed and expected mean nearest-neighbor distance (miles)
ann_obs <- mean(nndist(station_pp))
ann_exp <- 0.5 / sqrt(npoints(station_pp) / area.owin(Window(station_pp)))
ann_obs / ann_exp

clarkevans.test(station_pp, correction = "none", alternative = "two.sided",
                method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
set.seed(391)
st_q <- quadratcount(station_pp, nx = 3, ny = 2)
st_qt <- quadrat.test(station_pp, nx = 3, ny = 2, method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
set.seed(391)
st_ce <- clarkevans.test(station_pp, correction = "none", alternative = "two.sided", method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
```

The two tests answer different questions. The VMR is `r fmt(var(as.vector(st_q)) / mean(as.vector(st_q)), 1)` (p = `r fmt(st_qt$p.value, 3)`), so stations are not spread evenly across the three counties. The ANN ratio is `r fmt(st_ce$statistic)` (p = `r fmt(st_ce$p.value, 2)`), so the distance from each station to its nearest neighbor is about what CSR would give, or a little larger.

## Part 2: Partner Practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners use all of North Carolina as the window. Partner A analyzes the `r nrow(nc_hosp)` licensed hospitals from [NC OneMap](https://www.nconemap.gov/datasets/hospitals), and Partner B analyzes the `r nrow(schools)` public high schools that reported an average SAT score. Each task tells you in parentheses which walkthrough step to reuse.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#the North Carolina window (both partners)
nc_outline <- st_union(nc_counties)

#Partner A: hospitals, projected to NC State Plane (feet)
nc_hosp <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1K7lH1U6oQQ6sWXIqxOeFUYbWjdnxqx5a") |>
  st_transform(2264)

#Partner B: public high schools (already in NC State Plane)
schools <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1i-C2PF3ajbpHTlavh3m1QbWNObpobprZ")
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A: Hospitals

1. Make a point pattern of the hospitals in the North Carolina window, in miles, with duplicates dropped. *(Step 1)*
2. Map the kernel density with the points on top. *(Step 2)*
3. Run `set.seed(391)`, then a quadrat test with `nx = 6, ny = 2`, and find the VMR. *(Step 3)*
4. Run `set.seed(391)`, then find the ANN ratio and its p-value. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your number of points, VMR, quadrat p-value, ANN ratio and ANN p-value to Part 3.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B: High Schools

1. Make a point pattern of the schools in the North Carolina window, in miles, with duplicates dropped. *(Step 1)*
2. Map the kernel density with the points on top. *(Step 2)*
3. Run `set.seed(391)`, then a quadrat test with `nx = 6, ny = 2`, and find the VMR. *(Step 3)*
4. Run `set.seed(391)`, then find the ANN ratio and its p-value. *(Step 4)*

When you finish, bring your number of points, VMR, quadrat p-value, ANN ratio and ANN p-value to Part 3.
:::
::::

| Pattern | Points | VMR | Quadrat p-value | ANN ratio | ANN p-value |

## Answer Key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
nc_outline <- st_union(nc_counties)
make_pp <- function(pts) unique(rescale.ppp(as.ppp(st_geometry(pts), W = as.owin(nc_outline)), 5280, "mile"))
run_all <- function(pp) {
  set.seed(391); q <- quadratcount(pp, nx = 6, ny = 2)
  qt <- quadrat.test(pp, nx = 6, ny = 2, method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
  set.seed(391); ce <- clarkevans.test(pp, correction = "none", alternative = "two.sided", method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
  list(n = npoints(pp), vmr = var(as.vector(q)) / mean(as.vector(q)), qp = qt$p.value, r = ce$statistic, rp = ce$p.value)
}
ka <- run_all(make_pp(nc_hosp))
kb <- run_all(make_pp(schools))
```

| Pattern | Points | VMR | Quadrat p-value | ANN ratio | ANN p-value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hospitals | `r ka$n` | `r fmt(ka$vmr, 1)` | `r fmt(ka$qp, 3)` | `r fmt(ka$r)` | `r fmt(ka$rp, 3)` |
| High schools | `r kb$n` | `r fmt(kb$vmr, 1)` | `r fmt(kb$qp, 3)` | `r fmt(kb$r)` | `r fmt(kb$rp, 3)` |

Monte Carlo p-values can shift slightly with a different seed or R version, and 0.002 is the smallest possible value with 999 simulations.

A good card says something like this. Both patterns have strong first-order structure: intensity is highest around Charlotte, the Triad and the Triangle, where most people live, and both quadrat tests reject CSR. At the second order they differ. Hospitals have an ANN ratio close to 1, so once you account for their number, each hospital is about as far from its nearest neighbor as a random pattern would give. One hypothesis is that hospitals serve whole counties or regions, which spaces them out. High schools are clustered (ANN ratio about `r fmt(kb$r)`), because cities need many schools close together, and districts build them where students live.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
nc_outline <- st_union(nc_counties)

#### Partner A: hospitals ####
nc_hosp <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1K7lH1U6oQQ6sWXIqxOeFUYbWjdnxqx5a") |>
  st_transform(2264)

hosp_pp <- as.ppp(st_geometry(nc_hosp), W = as.owin(nc_outline))
hosp_pp <- rescale.ppp(hosp_pp, 5280, "mile")
hosp_pp <- unique(hosp_pp)

plot(density(hosp_pp), main = "Hospitals per square mile")
plot(hosp_pp, add = TRUE, pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

set.seed(391)
hosp_q <- quadratcount(hosp_pp, nx = 6, ny = 2)
var(as.vector(hosp_q)) / mean(as.vector(hosp_q))
quadrat.test(hosp_pp, nx = 6, ny = 2, method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)

set.seed(391)
mean(nndist(hosp_pp)) / (0.5 / sqrt(npoints(hosp_pp) / area.owin(Window(hosp_pp))))
clarkevans.test(hosp_pp, correction = "none", alternative = "two.sided",
                method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)

#### Partner B: high schools ####
schools <- st_read("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1i-C2PF3ajbpHTlavh3m1QbWNObpobprZ")

school_pp <- as.ppp(st_geometry(schools), W = as.owin(nc_outline))
school_pp <- rescale.ppp(school_pp, 5280, "mile")
school_pp <- unique(school_pp)

plot(density(school_pp), main = "High schools per square mile")
plot(school_pp, add = TRUE, pch = 16, cex = 0.5)

set.seed(391)
school_q <- quadratcount(school_pp, nx = 6, ny = 2)
var(as.vector(school_q)) / mean(as.vector(school_q))
quadrat.test(school_pp, nx = 6, ny = 2, method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)

set.seed(391)
mean(nndist(school_pp)) / (0.5 / sqrt(npoints(school_pp) / area.owin(Window(school_pp))))
clarkevans.test(school_pp, correction = "none", alternative = "two.sided",
                method = "MonteCarlo", nsim = 999)
```
